The visualization is built and checked in both light and dark mode. Open `kelvin-wave-2026.html` in a browser (a full-page render is in `preview-light.png`).

**What a Kelvin wave is**

A Kelvin wave is a very large, slow ocean wave that travels along a boundary. In the Pacific the boundary is either the equator, where the Coriolis effect changes sign, or a coastline. When trade winds weaken during a developing El Niño, warm water piled up in the western Pacific is released and travels east along the equator as a thick warm layer. It pushes the thermocline down and lifts the sea surface by inches to a foot across thousands of miles, taking two to three months to cross the basin. When it reaches the Americas the energy splits into coastally trapped waves that run poleward along the coast, one branch north past Mexico and California and one south along Peru and Chile.

**What is in the news this month**

- A northward coastal Kelvin wave is off Mexico, moving about 6 mph. Satellite altimetry showed it lifted Central American sea level 9 to 14 inches above the 1993 to 2025 average.
- Forecasters quoted by ABC7 and The Weather Channel expect a 6 to 12 inch lift in Southern California in early October, and CBS San Francisco reports roughly a foot in the Bay Area in the first or second week of October. Elevated water lingers for weeks, and the main worry is coastal flooding and erosion when winter storms and the Thanksgiving and Christmas king tides arrive on top of it.
- NOAA's September 10 ENSO discussion has an El Niño Advisory in effect, with a 75 percent chance the October to December value tops +2.5 °C, which would be the strongest since 1950.

**What the page contains**

- A stat row with the headline numbers, and an SVG cross-section schematic showing the equatorial wave, thermocline, and coastal split.
- A Pacific-centered map with the equatorial wave path, the four Niño index regions labeled with NOAA's September 9 anomalies, the northward coastal branch, and hover dots for each place with an observed or forecast sea-level lift.
- An arrival timeline from Central America to the Pacific Northwest, with observed, forecast, and unquantified windows kept visually distinct.
- Two comparison charts of weekly Niño-3.4 and Niño-1+2 anomalies for 2026 against 1997 and 2015, from NOAA's live index file. 2026 is ahead of both at the same point in the year.
- Tide-gauge charts for San Francisco and La Jolla from NOAA's CO-OPS API, showing both gauges already 3 to 5 inches above their monthly norms before the wave arrives.
- A world map and table of downstream El Niño effects, with shape and color encoding wet, dry, and ocean impacts, and a bold ring marking effects reported this month versus typical historical patterns.

Every chart has tooltips, a table view, a legend, and a dark-mode toggle. The three-color palette passed the dataviz validator for colorblind separation in both modes. Two caveats are noted on the page: the Cabo San Lucas lift is interpolated rather than reported, and gauge anomalies include a small long-term sea-level-rise component.

Sources: [NOAA CPC ENSO Diagnostic Discussion](https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/analysis_monitoring/enso_advisory/ensodisc.shtml), [ABC7 Los Angeles](https://abc7.com/post/el-nio-related-kelvin-wave-headed-socal-could-bring-dangerously-high-sea-levels/19824476/), [CBS San Francisco](https://www.cbsnews.com/sanfrancisco/news/bay-area-sea-levels-kelvin-wave-pacific-ocean-el-nino/), [The Weather Channel](https://weather.com/2026/09/12/safety/floods/el-nino-kelvin-wave-california-sea-levels-flooding-winter-fall), [CNN Climate](https://www.cnn.com/climate/el-nino-california-sea-levels-coastal-flooding), [Above the Norm News](https://www.abovethenormnews.com/2026/09/03/el-nino-kelvin-wave-2026/), [IRI ENSO Quick Look](https://iri.columbia.edu/our-expertise/climate/forecasts/enso/current/), [NOAA weekly Niño indices](https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/data/indices/wksst9120.for).
